Jun 2023 exam: full worked solutions

How to use this: sit it timed first (120 min, open book). Do not open this until time is up.

Then mark yourself part by part. The course only gives final numbers for this paper, so the mark splits below are suggested splits based on the marks printed on the paper, not an official marking scheme. Every number here was computed in Python and checked against “eec jun23 exam numerical answers”. Where the official sheet differs (a typo or a rounding), the solution says so.

Exam technique for this paper

Time. 80 marks in 120 minutes is 1.5 minutes per mark, so 30 minutes per question. Leave 5 minutes at the end to check angles and units.

Part Marks Time Difficulty
1a battery 5 6 min easy
1b star/delta 6 8 min easy
1c RLC phasors 9 14 min medium (long, but routine)
2a magnetics 9 13 min medium
2b transformer tests 5 8 min easy
2c transformer equations 6 8 min medium (words and formulas)
3a AC machine basics 6 8 min easy
3b and sketch 5 8 min medium
3c IM torque and current 9 13 min medium
4a synchronous generator 5 8 min medium
4b PFC with a synchronous motor 7 11 min medium
4c short answers 8 10 min easy if you know the points

Where the easy marks are. 1a, 1b, 2b, 3a(i)–(ii), 3c(i)–(ii), 4b(i)–(ii) are about 25 marks of one- or two-line answers. Bank them first if you are nervous. 4c is 8 marks for words only, so do not leave it to the last 2 minutes.

What to write for method marks.

  • Write the formula in symbols first, then the numbers, then the answer with units. A wrong final number with the right formula usually keeps most of the marks.
  • Say what each value is: “phase voltage V”. Star/delta and per-phase mistakes are the most common loss on this paper.
  • Give phasors in polar form when the question says “polar form” (1c), and always give the angle sign.
  • In the IM and synchronous parts, state the slip, and the bases before using them.
  • For “explain” parts (2c(iii), 3a(ii), 3c(ii), 4c), give a reason, not just the answer. “Generator, because so ” earns the mark. “Generator” alone may not.

4c) Short-Answer Questions [8 marks]

Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without using any sketches, drawings or equations).

i) Explain the concept of power-factor correction. Why is power-factor correction useful in power systems? [ 3 marks ]

ii) Carefully explain the differences and similarities between transformers and induction machines. [ 3 marks ]

iii) Consider a squirrel-cage induction machine. If the rotor cage was made from a perfect conductor (with infinite conductivity) how would this affect the properties of the machine? [ 2 marks ]

Model answers

(i) Power-factor correction. Many loads, such as induction motors and transformers, draw reactive power as well as real power. Reactive power is energy that oscillates back and forth between the supply and the load each cycle. It does no useful work, but it increases the current. This extra current loads up generators, transformers and lines, uses up their rating, and causes extra copper losses and voltage drop. Power-factor correction means adding a source of reactive power close to the load, usually a capacitor bank connected in parallel with it (or an over-excited synchronous machine). The capacitor generates the reactive power the load needs, so less reactive power is drawn from the supply. The supply current falls for the same real power, the power factor moves towards one, and losses and charges for poor power factor are reduced.

(ii) Transformers and induction machines. Similarities: both can operate from a three-phase AC supply. Both have a primary (stator) winding and a secondary (rotor) winding coupled by a magnetic core. Both have nearly the same equivalent circuit, with winding resistances, leakage reactances, a magnetising reactance and a core-loss resistance, and both can be analysed per phase with a simplified circuit. Differences: in an induction machine the secondary winding is on the rotor, which turns, and it is short-circuited rather than feeding a load. The rotor frequency is the slip times the stator frequency, so it differs from the supply frequency. An induction machine also has an airgap, so its magnetising current is much larger. In the induction machine equivalent circuit, the referred rotor resistance is divided by the slip. This term represents both the rotor copper loss and the mechanical output power.

(iii) Perfectly conducting rotor. The rotor resistance would be zero. There would be no rotor copper loss, so efficiency would be higher. The rotor would carry whatever current is needed at almost exactly synchronous speed. The torque–speed curve would become vertical at synchronous speed, like a synchronous machine, so the speed would hardly change with load. But the machine would produce no torque away from synchronous speed, so it would have zero starting torque and could not start on its own. (This is the limit of the Q3b sketch as rotor resistance goes to zero: the peak moves right up to synchronous speed.)

Marks: (i) 1 what reactive power is and why it is a problem, 1 capacitor in parallel generates reactive power, 1 the benefit (lower current, losses, better use of rating). (ii) about 1.5 for similarities, 1.5 for differences (rotating short-circuited secondary, different rotor frequency, ). (iii) 1 for “zero , no rotor loss, higher efficiency”, 1 for “vertical τ–n curve at and zero starting torque”.

Common mistake: in (iii), saying the machine would be “more efficient” and stopping there. The second mark needs the zero starting torque. In all of 4c, do not draw a phasor diagram or write a formula: the question forbids it.
